lead: Grover's algorithm searches an unstructured list of N items for one marked item using about √N quantum queries instead of N classical checks. Here N=2<sup>n</sup>, and n is the number of qubits. An oracle flips the sign of the marked item. A diffusion operator then inverts all amplitudes about their mean. Repeating the pair boosts the marked amplitude. This is a quadratic speedup, not an exponential one. Some syllabi call it Grover's quantum search algorithm. It is used for search, constraint solving and brute-force tasks where no structure gives a faster classical method.
prereq: You need: phase kickback from 4.1, and Hadamard gates and oracle construction from Unit 3.

blocks.text: A list has N items, labelled x=0,1,...,N−1. Exactly one item w is marked. A classical algorithm that checks one item per query needs N queries in the worst case, and about N/2 on average. The list has no order, so binary search does not apply. Grover uses n=log₂N qubits, so N=2<sup>n</sup>. The input state is the uniform superposition |s⟩ = (1/√N) Σ<sub>x</sub> |x⟩.
The quantum query is an oracle. It changes only the sign of the marked item; all other items keep their sign. Phase kickback from 4.1 turns a Boolean oracle into this sign flip.
U<sub>w</sub>|x⟩ = (−1)<sup>f(x)</sup>|x⟩, with f(x)=1 if x=w and f(x)=0 otherwise
blocks.where: U<sub>w</sub> is the oracle; x is a list index from 0 to N−1; w is the marked index; f(x) is the marking function.

blocks.text: In the first iteration, after the oracle the marked amplitude is 1/√N in magnitude and negative, and all other amplitudes are positive. Let the current amplitudes be a<sub>x</sub>. The diffusion operator D maps a<sub>x</sub> to 2⟨a⟩ − a<sub>x</sub>, where ⟨a⟩ is the mean of all N amplitudes. A negative marked amplitude pulls the mean down slightly. In that first iteration, the map turns the marked amplitude positive and larger, and turns each unmarked amplitude slightly smaller.

In matrix form D = 2|s⟩⟨s| − I, where |s⟩ is the uniform superposition and I is the identity. The circuit builds D as H<sup>⊗n</sup>(2|0⟩⟨0|−I)H<sup>⊗n</sup>. One oracle plus one D is one Grover iteration G = D U<sub>w</sub>. The state stays in the plane spanned by |w⟩ and the uniform superposition of all unmarked items; the other N−2 directions are never populated.

sections.h3: The Grover iteration as a rotation

blocks.text: Define |α⟩ = (1/√(N−1)) Σ<sub>x≠w</sub> |x⟩, the uniform state over unmarked items. The start state is |s⟩ = sin θ |w⟩ + cos θ |α⟩, with sin θ = 1/√N. The angle θ = arcsin(1/√N) is measured in radians. One Grover iteration rotates the state by 2θ in this plane.

blocks.where: P(k) is the probability of measuring the marked item after k iterations; θ is the angle with sin θ = 1/√N; N is the number of items; k is the number of Grover iterations.

blocks.text: After k iterations, the amplitude of |w⟩ is sin((2k+1)θ), so the success probability is P(k). Set (2k+1)θ ≈ π/2 for the first peak. Then k<sub>opt</sub> ≈ (π/4)√N − 1/2, which is about (π/4)√N for large N.

items: Repeat k times: apply the oracle U<sub>w</sub>, then the diffusion operator D.
Measure all qubits in the computational basis.

blocks.text: Grover needs about (π/4)√N oracle calls and about the same number of diffusion steps. The classical worst case is N checks, so the speedup is quadratic: N=10<sup>12</sup> needs about 10<sup>6</sup> Grover steps, not 10<sup>12</sup>. This is not exponential. The oracle must be a real quantum circuit whose cost is counted; a classical check of each item gains nothing.

The method is used for unstructured search, for brute-force search over candidate solutions, and as amplitude amplification inside larger algorithms. Extra iterations reduce the success probability after the first peak, so k is chosen in advance. Quantum counting and the √N lower bound are in 4.8.

figure.caption: With θ = arcsin(1/4), the success probability sin²((2k + 1)θ) climbs 0.0625, 0.4727, 0.9084 to 0.9613 at k = 3, then falls if more iterations are run.

examples.question: N=16 items, one marked item. Use θ=arcsin(1/√16). Find the success probability after k=0,1,2,3 Grover iterations. Which k in this set is best, and what is P at that k?
steps: Compute θ = arcsin(1/√16) = arcsin(0.25) = 0.252680 rad ≈ 0.2527 rad.
For each k, the angle is (2k+1)θ: k=0: 0.2527 rad; k=1: 0.7580 rad; k=2: 1.2634 rad; k=3: 1.7688 rad.
At k=3, P=0.9613, so measurement returns the marked item with probability 96.13%.
examples.answer: For N=16 the best k is 3, with success probability P≈0.9613 (96.13%).
examples.check:
import math
N = 16
theta = math.asin(1 / math.sqrt(N))
print(round(theta, 4))
for k in range(4):
    p = math.sin((2 * k + 1) * theta) ** 2
    print(round(p, 4))

traps: Stopping at the first peak matters. Running more than k<sub>opt</sub> rotations moves the state past |w⟩ and lowers P(k).
The oracle is a unitary quantum query. A classical loop that checks each item is not a Grover oracle and gives no speedup.
Do not mix N and n. N is the number of items; n=log₂N is the number of qubits; θ uses √N.
The formula is sin²((2k+1)θ), not sin²(2kθ). At k=0 it must give 1/N.
Diffusion is inversion about the mean, not about zero. The negative sign on the marked amplitude is what makes the mean shift.

quiz.q: What does the Grover oracle do to the marked item?
quiz.a: It multiplies the marked item's amplitude by −1; other amplitudes are unchanged.

quiz.q: Why does diffusion increase the marked amplitude?
quiz.a: The negative marked amplitude lowers the mean. Inverting every amplitude about that mean makes the marked amplitude positive and larger.

quiz.q: For N=64, sin θ=1/8. Estimate k<sub>opt</sub>.
Why can extra Grover iterations reduce success probability?
quiz.a: Each iteration is a rotation by 2θ. After the first peak near π/2, more rotations move the state away from |w⟩.

quiz.q: Write P(k) and the equation for θ.
For N=16, what is P at k=1?
What is the quadratic speedup in Grover search?
quiz.a: Classical search needs O(N) queries; Grover needs O(√N) oracle calls.

quiz.q: Why does Grover not solve NP-complete problems in polynomial time?
quiz.a: The speedup is quadratic, not exponential. For a search space of size 2m, Grover still needs about 2m/2 queries; see 4.8.

beyond: Not for the exam. Amplitude amplification generalizes Grover: any algorithm that can prepare a good state with probability p can be boosted using about 1/√p iterations. Quantum counting uses phase estimation on the Grover operator to estimate the number of marked items. The √N lower bound shows no quantum algorithm can do better for an unstructured oracle, up to constants. Search ideas also appear in collision finding and in some constraint solvers. Search next for amplitude amplification and quantum walk search.
